name: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
title: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
answer: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the practice of translating how an AI system reaches its outputs into language and evidence that non-specialists can assess. It spans both external audiences, such as supervisors and customers, and internal ones, such as risk committees and auditors. The work includes model documentation, feature importance summaries, decision rationales, and records of how a model was validated. It sits inside governance and fiduciary risk because a firm's duty of care depends on being able to show that a model behaves as intended and that its limits are understood.

sections.body: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the practice of translating how an AI system reaches its outputs into language and evidence that non-specialists can assess. It spans both external audiences, such as supervisors and customers, and internal ones, such as risk committees and auditors. The work includes model documentation, feature importance summaries, decision rationales, and records of how a model was validated. It sits inside governance and fiduciary risk because a firm's duty of care depends on being able to show that a model behaves as intended and that its limits are understood.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the same infrastructure that builds and operates models, plus layers for logging, versioning, and documentation. Model registries, experiment trackers, and data lineage tools capture what data was used and which model version produced a given output. Explanation outputs are often stored alongside model artifacts and served through dashboards or reporting systems that regulators and clients can access. In many firms, the final delivery still relies on structured documents and spreadsheets that combine technical metrics with plain language commentary.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method starts by defining the decision or output that needs explaining and the audience that will receive the explanation. Teams then choose appropriate techniques, such as global feature importance for overall behavior and local explanations for individual cases, and they test whether those explanations are stable and faithful to the model. A crucial step is validation with domain experts, legal reviewers, and sometimes client representatives to ensure the explanation is accurate and not misleading. The final product is usually a layered set of materials, from a short summary for executives to a detailed appendix for technical reviewers.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this area turn on data provenance, consent, and the audit trail that supports each explanation. Firms must track where training data came from, how it was transformed, and which model version produced a given decision, because regulators and clients may challenge the explanation later. The site tracks 148 active AI lawsuits, which shows that unclear or inconsistent explanations can become a source of dispute. Provenance also covers the explanation itself, including who approved it, when it was generated, and whether it has been updated after a model change.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more standardized and more frequent explanation, similar to how financial disclosures became routine. Regulators are moving from principles to specific documentation requirements, and clients are asking for model explanations as part of due diligence. Automation will play a larger role, with tools that generate draft explanations from model metadata and logs, but human review will remain necessary for context and judgment. Over time, the ability to explain a model clearly may become a condition for deploying it in regulated markets.
